newsitem.title: HONG KONG: WEEK AHEAD - Hong Kong stocks brace for handover par.
newsitem.headline: WEEK AHEAD - Hong Kong stocks brace for handover par.

text.p: The Hong Kong stock market is expected to mark a new era under China on Thursday with a liquidity-driven surge, as a flow of mainland money rushes into the territory to celebrate its return to Chinese rule.

Britain will hand Hong Kong back to China on midnight on Monday after 156 years of colonial rule. The market will be closed from Monday to Wednesday to celebrate the event. For the stock market, the party will begin on Thursday, analysts said.
"We may see a celebration rally on the first day," said Geoff Galbraith, institutional sales trader at NAVA SC Securities.
Brokers are predicting heavy participation from mainland investors who want to mark the new era with a buoyant market.
Red chips should be under the spotlight as investors anticipate a brighter future for the mainland-controlled Hong Kong-based companies under China.
"It seems like we will see a new era with the red flag and the red chips flying," said Howard Gorges, vice chairman at South China Holdings.

The red chip Hang Seng China-Affiliated Corporations Index marked the final day of trading under colonial rule last Friday with a surge of 224.63 points, or 6.92 percent, to 3,469.32 points, its biggest point gain since it was launched on June 16.
The blue chip Hang Seng Index ended at a record closing high, gaining 68.77 points, or 0.45 percent, to 15,196.79.
Over the week it advanced 42.43 points, or 0.28 percent.
With the handover holiday period ahead, and a U.S. Federal Reserve policy-setting meeting scheduled for Tuesday and Wednesday, analysts said some investors had been cautious.
But money sitting on the sidelines should come rushing into the market next week if the change in sovereignty goes smoothly and U.S. interest rates remain steady, they said.

"Barring any major mishap between now and Thursday, the market is going to go up," said Miles Remington, sales trader at SocGen-Crosby Securities. "If rates are raised and Wall Street reacts negatively, blue chips may go down and red chips up."

Weak property stocks, which weighed on the Hang Seng Index last Friday, could see a pick up next week if Hong Kong's new government gives some indication of its future housing policy, clearing recent uncertainty in the market, analysts said.
China's plan to deploy 4,000 troops in Hong Kong just six hours after the territory returns to China should not unsettle the mood, they added.
"It's good that it is July 1 and not July 3 because people will calm down by then although they may have emotional feelings," said Frederick Tsang, head of research at BNP PrimeEast Securities.
